title: Quiet Compass — candidate reflection (runtime infra)
content:
Quick context
- Interview loop today: 60m system design + 45m on a take-home debrief. Candidate: 'quiet-compass' (prefers to go by QC). Senior infra engineer with 5y in production inference stacks, most recent at a scaling startup.

Immediate impressions (gut)
- Calm, measured communicator; speaks in constraints and tradeoffs instead of immediate yes/no.
- Strong practical instincts around cache invalidation and KV cache size heuristics.
- Slightly conservative on adopting new quantization/3rd-party kernels — favors reproducibility and observability.

Strengths (concrete)
- Latency sensitivity: suggested a prefix KV eviction policy tied to 95th percentile sequence length rather than fixed token count (good real-world nuance).
- Observability-first ops: advocated inexpensive distributed tracing sampling + token-level cost attribution; proposed a pragmatic rollout instrumentation plan that maps directly to our console dashboards.
- Pragmatic decomposition: can propose incremental changes with clear rollback hooks (A/B rollout -> canary -> global).

Risks / red flags
- Limited recent exposure to custom CUDA kernels and Triton internals — has experience with tuned OpenAI/RW-style kernels but not deep low-level optimization. Could be slower learning curve for serving-runtime kernel work.
- Strong adherence to “small, well-instrumented releases”; might push back on aggressive optimization experiments when product needs quick unit-cost wins. This is a culture fit tradeoff, not strictly negative.
- Interview-didn't-expand: when I pushed on autoscaling heuristics under cold-start heavy traffic (cold model load + bursty traffic), response stayed high-level. Did not sketch explicit control loops or backpressure plumbing.

Behavioral / culture fit
- Team player, mentions pairing frequently and likes asynchronous writeups.
- Values reproducibility and postmortems; has run runbooks and incident drills.
- Soft signal: tends to frame problems from past pain (safety of existing infra) — could be great for reliability but may slow risky experiments.

Technical notes and probes to verify if we move forward
- Follow-up takehome: ask candidate to design a fallback routing strategy that gracefully degrades model fidelity while preserving latency SLOs across Dedicated and Hosted. Specifically evaluate: cost accounting, KV cache reuse, and cold-start mitigation.
- Kernel/quantization homework: a short explainer of a quantization tradeoff they would propose for a 13B model on A100 vs L40; ask for expected perf numbers and test plan.
- Autoscale control loop sketch: request a small state diagram / pseudo-code for how they’d implement scale-up/scale-down with queued request backpressure and model spin-up delay.

Suggested rating (quick heuristic)
- Tech depth (serving infra): 7/10 (good system design, weaker in low-level kernels)
- Production-readiness / ops: 9/10
- Collaboration / communication: 8/10
- Overall hire inclination: green-yellow (would be comfortable hiring for a role focused on reliability/ops; for a kernel-focused IC role I’d want complementary hires or training budget)

Potential interviewer calibration notes (for hiring committee)
- If hiring manager prioritizes kernel/low-level work: highlight the kernel gap and propose pairing weeks + internal project rotation to upskill.
- If hiring manager needs immediate SRE/routing/observability owner: candidate matches well and could own runbooks, rollout policies, and cost attribution.

Ramp / onboarding sketch (30-60-90)
- 0–30 days: shadow on-call, replicate a single perf regression in a sandbox, run a basic canary deploy with tracing enabled.
- 30–60 days: lead a small rollout for a caching change (eviction heuristic) and measure unit-cost impact in the console.
- 60–90 days: own a cross-team runbook for fallback routing between Hosted and Dedicated variants and propose a quantization experiment.

Compensation & availability notes (asked during call)
- Target window: available in 4–6 weeks; current comp expectations region-aligned (no concrete number given).

Open questions I still have
- Depth on CUDA/Triton: they said 'some exposure' — need concrete repo examples or PRs.
- Experience with private deployments/VPC: they mentioned a single on-prem migration 3y ago but not owning long-lived private stacks.
- Comfort with driving product tradeoffs where unit-cost optimization may increase output noise (we need someone who can balance fallbacks and quality).

Next steps I propose
- Send two follow-ups (ASAP): 1) the autoscale control loop sketch (quick takehome), 2) kernel/quantization explainer (short doc + perf hypothesis). Ask for git links or PRs if available.
- If answers are solid, move to manager loop focused on kernel-upskilling plan and alignment to team goals.

Notes to self (meta)
- Use candidate as checklist for building an ops-focused hire profile: good to have at least one person who will defend reproducibility and keep SLOs from regressing.
- Keep interview questions that elicit low-level tradeoffs for future loops: e.g., "show me a repo commit where you fixed a caching correctness bug under heavy concurrency."

End of notes.
